# Transforming Code Reviews with AI

## Features

**Automated Reviews**: Continuous reviews of the pull requests including incremental commits. 

**Summarization**: Generates high-level summary and a technical walkthrough of the PR changes. 

**Line-by-line review**: Provides line-by-line suggestions committable with one click.

**Codebase verification**:  Verifies the impact on the overall codebase and identifies missing changes.

**Insights into your code**:  Ask any questions on your codebase within the pull request 

**Chat about your code** : Chat with the bot around your code. The more you chat, the smarter it gets.

**Issue Validation**:  Validates the PR against the linked issues and identifies other related issues

body: Hmm, I see this as another red flag, very similar to the timer thread. You are likely hitting this because you have the select degrade into a non-yielding loop. I'd consider calling maybeYield in the select fast path, which would enforce occasional polls and allow other tasks to run. Or maybe even direct yield, as one scheduler cycle per select is expected anyway.

Sorry, i misunderstood one part of this.

I think the best option is updating the cache now after returning from backend.

Or possible after each timer add, but I'd prefer to stay away from that. If we go that way, I'd remove the cached time completely.

We tested both suggested shapes before replying, on upstream main (4f831ea), with a detector at the arm site that reports any `.duration` deadline already >100 ms in the past against a fresh clock read. Three full h2spec runs per variant:

| variant | backdated arms | the affected case |
|---|---|---|
| main, unchanged | 3 of 3 runs | fails 3 of 3 |
| `maybeYield()` at select entry | 1 of 3 | fails 1 of 3 |
| `yield()` at select entry | 3 of 3 | fails 3 of 3 |
| forced `.reschedule` yield at select entry | 1 of 3 | fails 1 of 3 |
| fresh clock read in `armTimer` (this PR) | 0 of 4 | passes 4 of 4 |

Every detector hit is the same timer: `dur_ms=5000, late_ms≈5000` — a 5 s select timeout armed ~10 s after the cache was last refreshed.

The shape we measured is also not a non-yielding loop. The backdated arm is the FIRST select of a freshly accepted connection: the executor's backend poll slept ~10 s because the server was idle (the conformance case sends nothing), woke on the accept, and the first task batch after the wake armed the timer. The regression test in this PR reproduces it without select at all — one pipe-read completion wakes a 1.2 s sleep, then a single `Loop.add` of a 500 ms timer fires in ~0 ms on main.

Why a yield cannot close it: the cache refresh lives in `checkTimers` at the top of `poll`, and after the backend poll only when it timed out. A yield moves the task to the back of the run queue the executor is currently draining; the executor does not poll between batch items. So the resumed task still arms inside the same post-wake batch, unless the tick budget happens to force a trip through `poll` first — which is why two of the variants reduce the rate without closing it.

An alternative that keeps the per-scan cache philosophy would be to call `updateNow()` whenever the backend poll returns from an actual wait, not only on timeout. That fixes the post-wake batch at one clock read per wake, but a long CPU-bound batch can still go stale under it. The arm-site read is the only shape where `.duration` means "from the arm call" unconditionally, at one `clock_gettime` per armed timer.

Happy to rework to the `updateNow`-on-wake shape if you prefer the cache-centric fix; the select fast-path fairness question sounds real but looks like a separate change either way.

The cache now is supposed to give illusion that tasks running within one tick are running concurrently. It got s bit more complex with work stealing, but I'd like to continue that. So if two tasks arm 0.1s timers, they should both fire at the same time, no matter if another task hogged the executor. I night need to further adjust this, bit I'd definitely go with updateNow after wake for now.

Reworked to your preferred shape (our comments crossed — the table above was written against the first comment). The PR now refreshes the snapshot with `updateNow()` right after a backend poll that could have waited (`backend_timeout != 0`), and `armTimer` is back to the cached read. A zero-timeout poll cannot sleep, so CPU-bound polling pays nothing new.

Verification on this shape: `zig build test` 653 of 653; the regression test fails without the patch and passes with it; the h2spec case that exposed this passes 4 of 4 full-suite runs (it failed 8 of 11 before).
